content: Gastroenteritis refers to the inflammation of the stomach, small intestine, and large intestine. Viral gastroenteritis is a condition caused by various viruses that leads to symptoms such as vomiting or diarrhea. Despite being commonly referred to as the stomach flu, it is not caused by influenza viruses. A wide range of viruses can cause viral gastroenteritis, including rotaviruses, noroviruses, adenovirus types 40 and 41, sapoviruses, and astroviruses. It is important to note that viral gastroenteritis is not caused by bacteria (e.g., Salmonella or Escherichia coli), parasites (e.g., Giardia), medications, or other medical conditions, even though the symptoms may resemble those caused by these factors. Rotavirus infections can be confirmed through laboratory testing of stool samples. However, routine diagnostic tests for other viruses that cause gastroenteritis are not commonly available. In special cases, the Viral Gastroenteritis Unit at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) can provide advanced diagnostic assistance upon request. The cornerstone of treatment for viral gastroenteritis in both children and adults is the prevention of dehydration. This management should ideally begin at home. Physicians may provide specific guidance on the types of fluids to administer. The CDC advises families with infants and young children to always have a supply of oral rehydration solution (ORS) at home and to use it as soon as diarrhea begins. Medications, including antibiotics (which are ineffective against viruses), should not be used unless explicitly recommended by a healthcare provider. For prevention, a licensed rotavirus vaccine is available and provides protection against severe diarrhea caused by rotavirus in infants and young children. Research is ongoing to develop a vaccine for norovirus. To reduce the risk of infection, individuals should practice frequent handwashing, promptly disinfect contaminated surfaces using household chlorine bleach-based cleaners, and immediately wash soiled clothing. If food or water is suspected to be contaminated, it should be avoided.
